description: Somos Lattices Team, un equipo de Antofagasta compuesto por dos desarrolladores, una ingeniera en Gestión de la Información, una ingeniera comercial spekear y un ingeniero civil con experiencia en pitch y storytelling. una Nuestro objetivo es identificar lugares terrestres análogos a futuras bases lunares y marcianas, usando datos abiertos y el desierto de Atacama. Unimos devs, análisis y ciencia. Buscamos colaborar con perfiles de geología, SIG/GIS, teledetección y ciencia de datos.
summary: CKEPI is a fully functional, deployed, open-source geospatial platform for exploring, analyzing, and identifying potential Earth analog sites for Moon and Mars research. It features operational frontend and backend systems, providing an integrated environment for planetary analog site exploration. Its first use case is preliminary site screening for rover-related field experiments. A multiresolution terrestrial grid helps users examine candidates, compare available environmental and terrain descriptors, and distinguish measurable similarities from physical conditions that an Earth location cannot reproduce. The application brings together interactive planetary views, an exploratory comparison engine, data-source information, and a student-oriented learning pathway. The team reports completed ingestion of terrestrial climate data and ongoing digital elevation enrichment; the direct, reproducible Jezero–Atacama terrain comparison remains to be verified. We aim to extend investigation beyond familiar analogs, including potentially under-characterized areas of Antofagasta, without claiming new discoveries or operational safety. CKEPI connects preliminary research questions with accessible planetary-science learning and openly documents its assumptions and limitations.
details:
The challenge and the problem

Earth analog sites can help researchers prepare and frame experiments related to future Moon and Mars exploration. Yet a visually Mars-like landscape may differ substantially in terrain geometry, climatic properties, geological context, or the physical conditions relevant to a particular experiment. Environmental and elevation datasets also vary by resolution, geographic coverage, units, provenance, and uncertainty. Focusing only on established analogs can overlook other Earth regions worth studying. No natural terrestrial site simultaneously reproduces another world's gravity, atmospheric environment, and radiation conditions.

What CKEPI is designed to solve

CKEPI helps users explore and preliminarily screen Earth candidate locations for particular scientific questions. The first application focus is rover-related field testing, not certifying rover traversability or mission safety. The platform asks: *Which site merits further investigation for this experiment, what evidence is available, and what information is missing?* Potential future mission profiles—such as research related to landing technology or controlled plant-growth experiments—would require different variables, screening criteria, and domain-specific validation. They are not claimed as completed capability.

Current platform and workflow

CKEPI's documented software organizes Earth candidates in a multiresolution H3 grid and provides interactive planetary views, candidate rankings, variable-by-variable comparisons, limitations, and results export. Users can select a target such as Mars' Jezero Crater, explore terrestrial candidates, inspect available descriptors, and view major physical non-equivalences. A reported student-oriented route is available at the team's deployment URL, while the complete guided learning workflow still requires functional and user validation.

The intended screening sequence is: (1) environmental context, including air/soil temperature, humidity, and other available climatic variables; (2) terrain context, including elevation-derived slope and roughness where sufficiently reliable DEM processing exists; (3) candidate assessment, documenting source, spatial scale, method, missing information, and a reason for further study. Each criterion must be interpreted according to the experiment's actual objective; no universal similarity percentage establishes that a site is 'Mars-like'.

Actual reported data-processing progress

The team reports completion of terrestrial historical climate-data ingestion through Open-Meteo ERA5-Land. At its last supplied technical checkpoint, a five-point elevation enrichment procedure was in progress using Copernicus DEM access through Open-Meteo, with NASA/METI ASTER configured as a fallback. The checkpoint showed 3,020 of 10,660 cells processed, not a completed or fully validated topographic dataset. Actual ASTER fallback calls have not been established by supplied logs. A coarser spatial sampling stencil must not be described as rover-scale obstacle detection.

For a direct Jezero–Atacama scientific comparison, the team's planned workflow names an Earth elevation product such as NASADEM_HGT V001 and the Mars 2020 Science Investigation CTX DEM mosaic distributed by USGS. It requires study areas of comparable physical extent, correct coordinate systems and elevation units, careful treatment of effective resolution, valid-data masks, slope and local-relief calculations, uncertainty reporting, and reproducible code. The completed real-data comparison has not been independently verified. A nominal 30 m output grid must not be mistaken for 30 m source detail if the Earth data actually used have coarser resolution.

NASA resources and their role

NASA planetary reference information is documented as informing the project's discussion of physical differences such as surface gravity and atmospheric pressure. The public source repository also describes interfaces for NASA Trek planetary mapping, NASA PDS/ODE data discovery, NASA Earthdata catalog queries, and NASA POWER climatology. These integrations should be distinguished from verified, executed data products in the deployed site. NASA POWER was listed as a subsequent enrichment phase in the team update; it is not presented here as a completed historical-climate ingestion.

Verification required for a strong NASA-data claim: identify at least one exact NASA product, layer, dataset, or observation actually exercised in the submitted application, the computation or visual inference it supports, and an observable or reproducible result. NASA planetary facts can support an explanation of non-equivalence, but they do not alone validate a terrain-candidate ranking.

Scientific transparency and limits

CKEPI separates potentially comparable terrain/environmental characteristics from important non-reproducible physical factors. Its reported matching scores and rankings are exploratory model outputs: they depend on chosen variables, completeness, weights, statistical methods, and scale. They are not validated probabilities of mission success, universal Mars-similarity percentages, proof of causality, or safety certifications. A candidate shown by software is not automatically a newly discovered or scientifically validated analog.

An internal pitch draft reports exploratory distances of 0.54 for Pampa Central and 3.32 for Yungay relative to a Jezero reference. This numerical claim is not used as a scientific finding in this submission draft because the supplied materials lack the metric definition and units, input DEM files, reference windows, processing code/commit, and reproducibility checks needed to verify it. The values may be added only once those details are documented.

Technology

The documented project architecture includes React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and MapLibre GL JS in the frontend; Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, H3, DuckDB, and GeoParquet in its data, API, and candidate-search workflow. The repository also describes numerical/statistical Python components, third-party data adapters, and CSV/GeoJSON/Markdown exports. The team's implementation documentation does not, on its own, establish that every integration, endpoint, user-control, or mobile accessibility feature passed live end-to-end tests.

Innovation, audiences, and potential impact

CKEPI's proposed innovation is a single evidence-aware workflow that combines (1) searching beyond familiar terrestrial analog locations, (2) explicit, dimension-by-dimension explanations of what can and cannot be meaningfully compared, and (3) a gradual Look → Compare → Investigate experience for learners and non-specialists. Its first focus is research questions involving rovers; subsequent mission types are possible extensions rather than validated modules. Proposed users include research teams, field-test planners, educators, students, and local science facilitators. Northern Chile offers a motivating regional context. A pilot with a school or library in Antofagasta is a proposed next step, not a confirmed partnership or completed educational experiment.

The project does not claim to reduce mission expenses, outperform existing scientific tools, establish operational landing-site safety, prove crop suitability, create jobs, reduce emissions, or improve educational outcomes without study-specific evidence. NASA, ESA, and other agencies are not collaborators or endorsers of CKEPI.
